newsitem.title: USA: US Feb trade gap correction lifts Q1 GDP forecasts.
newsitem.headline: US Feb trade gap correction lifts Q1 GDP forecasts.

text.p: A billion-dollar correction by the Commerce Department to its headline February trade figure late on Thursday sent economists scuttling to add back most, if not all, of the cuts made to estimates of first-quarter real Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
"These numbers now tell us there wasn't as much deterioration in the trade balance as we thought yesterday morning," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities Inc, on Friday.

"On a preliminary basis, we calculate the deterioration in trade will hold GDP growth to about 4.3 to 4.4 percent," he said. Resler had approximated first quarter GDP growth at 4.5 percent before the trade figures.
Estimates of first quarter economic growth were pumped up almost half a percentage point earlier this week by strong U.S. consumer price, inventory and industrial production data, analysts said.

The ax fell on Thursday when the Commerce Department initially reported that imports increased a surprisingly strong 2.1 percent, causing the overall trade gap to shrink less than expected after an unusually large surge in January.
However, late Thursday Commerce said that after correcting for reporting errors on oil imports, the February deficit actually dropped 17.9 percent to $10.4 billion from $12.67 billion in January.
Initially, Commerce had reported an 8.5 percent narrowing in February to $11.59 billion gap, far above Wall Street expectations for a $10.1 billion deficit.
The initial February figure incorrectly included about $1.1 billion of oil imports that entered the country earlier and had to be subtracted from the estimate, Commerce said.

"In response to yesterday's surprisingly high, first-published deficit, we reduced our first quarter GDP estimate from 4.0 to 3.6 percent," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
"The correction to the February trade deficit implies that we will go right back to where we started yesterday morning -- 4.0 percent growth in real GDP for the first quarter," he added.
Despite the adjustment, economists said the first few months of 1997 showed significant deterioration in trade compared to the last quarter of 1996 when trade actually boosted GDP figures.
"It's still going to act as a drag on GDP, the question is how much," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Experts attributed the deterioration in the U.S. trade balance to a booming economy sucking up imports. Both imports and exports were at relatively high levels in early 1997, analysts said.
Economists eagerly awaited the full Commerce Department release of all revisions, scheduled for Friday, before finalizing their GDP forecasts.
Imports for months back as far as November 1995 had been included in the February total, meaning that figures in prior months may have been revised as well, they said.
